paper.title: The effect of influenza vaccination on the rate of dementia amongst older adults
paper.code_data_availability: DATA AVAILABILITY STATEMENT: 'This study is based entirely on anonymized personal data in the Danish national registries. …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish National Prescription Register (also called the Danish National Prescription Registry)
variables_mentioned: redeemed prescription for an influenza vaccine
anti-dementia medication: donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine, memantine (ATC N06DA02-N06DA04, N06DA52, N06DA53, N06DX01)
comorbidity ATC codes C02-C04, C07-C09 (hypertension), C10 (hyperlipidaemia), C01B (cardiac arrhythmia), A10A, A10B (diabetes), N04 (Parkinson's disease)
inpatient or outpatient dementia diagnosis of any type (ICD-8 290.09-290.19, 293.09-19; ICD-10 F00-F03, G30, G31)
comorbidity ICD-8 and ICD-10 codes listed in Table A1
inpatient or outpatient dementia diagnosis of any type

linkages: All Danish nationwide registries linked through the personal identifier given to all legal residents in Denmark [16]
Vaccination identified from either the Danish National Health Service Register or the Danish National Prescription Register
Dementia identified from either the Danish National Patient Register, the Danish Psychiatric Central Research Register or anti-dementia prescriptions in the Danish National Prescription Registry

sample.universe: All Danish residents aged >=65 years on 1 September 2002, or turning 65 years between 1 September 2002 and 31 August 2018 (N: 1,858,059)
sample.unit_of_observation: person-time (1-year age by 1-year calendar-year intervals); event counts modelled with the logarithm of person-years at risk as offset
selection_rules: Included from 1 September 2002 or, if younger than 65 years at that time, on their 65th birthday through rolling entry
Excluded due to dementia diagnosis before inclusion (N: 33,827), leaving 1,824,232
Excluded due to receiving an influenza vaccination before inclusion (N: 150,811), leaving a final study population of N = 1,673,421
People with mild cognitive impairment were not excluded
Followed from age >=65 until dementia diagnosis, emigration or death

Sensitivity subpopulation: individuals living in the municipality of Copenhagen at any time between 1996 and inclusion were excluded, and individuals were censored on the date they moved to Copenhagen after inclusion (about 6% fewer person-years and about 10% fewer dementia cases)
sample.n_observations: 14,065,154 person-years (135,399 dementia diagnoses; crude incidence rate 9.6 per 1000 person-years)
sample.n_individuals: 1,673,421 (991,729 vaccinated and 681,692 not vaccinated at inclusion; 6,549,905 vaccinated and 7,515,249 unvaccinated person-years)

construction_notes: Influenza vaccination assessed in three ways: (1) ever versus never vaccinated during follow-up; (2) number of vaccinations during follow-up in five categories (0, 1, 2, 3-5, >=6); (3) time between first influenza vaccination and dementia diagnosis, within or after 1, 2 and 5 years since vaccination
Vaccination is a time-dependent variable: individuals could contribute risk time as both unvaccinated and vaccinated depending on if and when they received their first influenza vaccination
Prescriptions redeemed before 2002 (register available from 1995) were very few and were used only to exclude people vaccinated before inclusion
Age and calendar year are the underlying time scales of the Poisson model, both in 1-year groups and included as time-dependent covariates

Sex and educational attainment assessed at the start of follow-up; education in four categories: high (short-term further education, bachelor's degree, research degree; >=12 years), medium (upper secondary, business high school, vocational internship; 10-12 years), low (primary school; <=9 years) and unknown
Marital status is a time-dependent covariate allowing multiple changes; it is available only at the end of each year, so the status date is approximated as 1 January of the following year

Comorbidities (stroke, cardiac arrhythmia, peripheral vascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, depression, alcohol use, Parkinson's disease) are time-dependent, persisting from first identification onwards; identified from a first inpatient or outpatient diagnosis, or a first redeemed prescription followed by a second within the following year (ATC codes registered at least twice within a 12-month period), and only where the drug is specific to that comorbidity

Crude incidence rate of dementia per 1000 person-years printed in Figure 3: 7.5 amongst the not vaccinated (56,387 cases) and 12.1 amongst the vaccinated (79,012 cases); by number of vaccinations 10.4 (1), 10.5 (2), 11.3 (3-5) and 14.6 (>=6); 9.9 within and 14.9 after five years of the first vaccination
Median age at dementia diagnosis 82.9 (Q1 78.1, Q3 87.4) amongst vaccinated and 81.6 (75.7, 86.6) amongst unvaccinated
Models: Model 1 adjusts for age, sex and calendar year; Model 2 adds marital status and educational attainment; Model 3 adds the comorbidities
SAS version 9.4 used for all statistical analyses; Figure 3 created using R version 4.2.2

links.pointer_quote: Vaccination during follow-up was associated with a slightly higher rate of dementia when adjusted for sociodemographic factors and comorbidities, both within and after the first 5 years from first vaccination (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.04; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.03–1.05).

claims.statement: Ever being vaccinated against influenza during follow-up is associated with a 4% higher all-cause dementia incidence rate than never being vaccinated, in the fully adjusted model.

treatment.label: Influenza vaccination during follow-up (ever versus never vaccinated)

register_source.value: Danish National Health Service Register (registered receipt of influenza vaccination) and Danish National Prescription Register (redeemed prescription for an influenza vaccine), both assessed from 2002 onwards

definition.value: Time-dependent indicator of having received at least one influenza vaccination during follow-up at age >=65, defined as a registered receipt of influenza vaccination in the Danish National Health Service Register or a redeemed prescription for an influenza vaccine in the Danish National Prescription Register, both assessed from 2002 onwards; individuals could contribute risk time as both unvaccinated and vaccinated depending on if and when they received their first vaccination. Reference: never vaccinated.

timing.value: Time-dependent during follow-up: person-time counts as unvaccinated until the date of the first influenza vaccination received at age >=65 between 1 September 2002 and 31 August 2018, and as vaccinated from that date onwards

register_source.value: Danish National Patient Register and Danish Psychiatric Central Research Register (inpatient or outpatient dementia diagnosis of any type) and Danish National Prescription Registry (first redeemed prescription for anti-dementia medication: donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine, memantine); ICD-8/ICD-10 and ATC codes listed in Table A1

definition.value: All-cause dementia defined as the first registered inpatient or outpatient diagnosis of any type in the Danish National Patient Register or the Danish Psychiatric Central Research Register, or the first redeemed prescription for anti-dementia medication in the Danish National Prescription Registry; analysed as an incidence rate with the logarithm of person-years at risk as offset. Crude incidence rate over the whole cohort: 9.6 per 1000 person-years (135,399 diagnoses in 14,065,154 person-years).

timing.value: First dementia diagnosis (or first anti-dementia prescription) during follow-up from inclusion at age >=65 until dementia diagnosis, emigration or death, 1 September 2002 to 31 August 2018

units.value: incidence rate ratio (IRR) relative to the reference category (not vaccinated / 0 vaccinations / no vaccination); 1 means equal incidence rates

magnitude.interpretation: A 4% higher incidence rate of dementia was found amongst ever vaccinated compared with never vaccinated in a fully adjusted model

estimand.target_population: Danish residents aged >=65 years in 2002-2018 who were free of dementia and had received no influenza vaccination before inclusion
estimand.time_horizon: Whole follow-up, 1 September 2002 to 31 August 2018 (up to 16 years from inclusion at age >=65)

population.description: Danish residents aged >=65 years, free of dementia and of any influenza vaccination at inclusion, followed from 1 September 2002 (or their 65th birthday) until dementia diagnosis, emigration or death, up to 31 August 2018
subgroups_defined: within versus after 1, 2 and 5 years since the first vaccination
subpopulation excluding inhabitants of the municipality of Copenhagen
population.selection: All Danish residents aged >=65 on 1 September 2002 or turning 65 by 31 August 2018 (N: 1,858,059), minus 33,827 with a dementia diagnosis before inclusion and 150,811 who had received an influenza vaccine before inclusion, giving a final study population of 1,673,421; people with mild cognitive impairment were not excluded

identification.source_of_variation: Observed differences in influenza vaccination uptake between older Danes in a nationwide cohort; vaccination has been offered free of charge to all Danish citizens aged >=65 since 2002, so there is no reform, lottery or discontinuity - identification rests entirely on adjustment for measured confounders

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the measured covariates (age, sex, calendar year, marital status, educational attainment and the nine comorbidities), vaccinated and unvaccinated person-time are comparable, so the adjusted incidence rate ratio has a causal reading; the covariates were selected as confounders of the vaccination-dementia association.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariates explicitly selected for their confounding potential; progressive adjustment across Models 1-3; the authors themselves conclude the assumption fails (residual confounding), citing the negative control outcomes and the higher mortality rate.

heterogeneity.finding: The rate of dementia decreased with increasing number of vaccinations; the highest rate was amongst those with only one vaccination and the only decreased rate amongst those with six or more (Table A2, Figure 3).
Inverse relation between age group and the dementia rate ratio: 11% higher at ages 65-74, 5% higher at 75-84 and 3% lower at ages >=85 (Table A6).
10% lower in 2002-2007, 7% higher in 2008-2013 and 18% higher in 2014-2018 (Table A7).
No considerable differences were found between the sex-stratified and main analyses (data not shown).
The rate was similarly increased within and after 1 year (6% and 3%), 2 years (5% and 3%) and 5 years (4% and 4%) since the first vaccination.

heterogeneity.finding: The IRRs of dementia, mortality and control outcomes were similar or identical in this subpopulation to those of the entire study population (Tables A8-A13).

ambiguities: The Results text on p. 4 gives the confidence interval for this estimate as 1.02-1.05 while Table 2 and Table A2 both print 1.03-1.05 (the abstract also prints 1.03-1.05); the table value is transcribed here.

The same ever-versus-never dementia estimate appears in Table 2 (Dementia as the outcome) and in Table A2 (Ever versus never vaccinated) and is plotted in Figure 3; the digest id cited is the one for the table the estimate is read from.

Estimand type is recorded as hazard_ratio because the schema has no rate-ratio category; the paper reports an incidence rate ratio from a Poisson model that it states is equivalent to a Cox regression.

Tables A8-A13 repeat these analyses in the subpopulation excluding inhabitants of the municipality of Copenhagen; they are recorded as robustness checks rather than as separate claims, as are Models 1 and 2.

value.claimed_domain: The risk of dementia from influenza vaccination in the general population of older adults, as against the preventive effect reported by some previous studies
boundary_conditions: The authors read their own positive association as residual confounding rather than an effect
Preventive effects could still exist for specific subpopulations
Vaccination at earlier ages than those studied (>=65 years) is not covered

theory_referenced: Proposal that common adult vaccines, including the influenza vaccine, may reduce the risk of dementia [2]
Infection and neuroinflammation as a pathway to cognitive impairment and incident dementia [3, 4]
Influenza vaccination reducing cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, which are risk factors for dementia [5, 6]
Increased amyloid-beta clearance through microglial activation in an Alzheimer's disease mouse model [7]
Healthy vaccinee effect / residual confounding by health status and health-seeking behaviour [34, 35]

prior_findings_compared.citation: Six observational studies reporting a lower risk of dementia amongst older adults receiving influenza vaccines [8-13]
prior_findings_compared.as_stated: Our findings did not align with any previous study in this area.

prior_findings_compared.citation: Douros et al. [14], common vaccines and the risk of incident dementia
prior_findings_compared.as_stated: The 39% higher odds of dementia amongst vaccinated people in one study [14] far exceeded the rate differences in the present study.

falsification.condition: The authors treat the negative control outcomes as the test: because the rates of cancer and hip fracture - assumed to be causally unrelated to vaccination - were also higher amongst vaccinated people, and mortality was higher too, the higher dementia rate is attributed to residual confounding rather than to an effect of vaccination.

outcomes_examined_not_reported: Sex-stratified analyses of the main association: 'No considerable differences were found between the sex-stratified and main analyses (data not shown)'

Incidence rate ratios with confidence intervals for dementia within and after 1 year and within and after 2 years since the first vaccination: percentages are given in the text but no estimates are tabulated ('data not shown')
Crude and adjusted person-years and case counts for the Copenhagen-excluded subpopulation ('data not shown'); only the percentage reductions of about 6% and 10% are given

treatment.label: Number of influenza vaccinations during follow-up: >=6 (versus 0)

register_source.value: Danish National Health Service Register (registered receipt of influenza vaccination) and Danish National Prescription Register (redeemed prescription for an influenza vaccine), both assessed from 2002 onwards

definition.value: Number of influenza vaccinations received during follow-up, in five categories (0, 1, 2, 3-5, >=6); this claim is category '>=6' compared with the reference category 0 (no vaccination during the study period). identification.source_of_variation: Observed differences in influenza vaccination uptake between older Danes in a nationwide cohort; vaccination has been offered free of charge to all Danish citizens aged >=65 since 2002, so there is no reform, lottery or discontinuity - identification rests entirely on adjustment for measured confounders

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the measured covariates (age, sex, calendar year, marital status, educational attainment and the nine comorbidities), vaccinated and unvaccinated person-time are comparable, so the adjusted incidence rate ratio has a causal reading; the covariates were selected as confounders of the vaccination-dementia association.

boundary_conditions: The authors read their own positive association as residual confounding rather than an effect
Preventive effects could still exist for specific subpopulations
Vaccination at earlier ages than those studied (>=65 years) is not covered

theory_referenced: Proposal that common adult vaccines, including the influenza vaccine, may reduce the risk of dementia [2]
Infection and neuroinflammation as a pathway to cognitive impairment and incident dementia [3, 4]
Influenza vaccination reducing cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, which are risk factors for dementia [5, 6]
Increased amyloid-beta clearance through microglial activation in an Alzheimer's disease mouse model [7]
Healthy vaccinee effect / residual confounding by health status and health-seeking behaviour [34, 35]

falsification.condition: The authors treat the negative control outcomes as the test: because the rates of cancer and hip fracture - assumed to be causally unrelated to vaccination - were also higher amongst vaccinated people, and mortality was higher too, the higher dementia rate is attributed to residual confounding rather than to an effect of vaccination.

outcomes_examined_not_reported: Sex-stratified analyses of the main association: 'No considerable differences were found between the sex-stratified and main analyses (data not shown)'

Incidence rate ratios with confidence intervals for dementia within and after 1 year and within and after 2 years since the first vaccination: percentages are given in the text but no estimates are tabulated ('data not shown')
Crude and adjusted person-years and case counts for the Copenhagen-excluded subpopulation ('data not shown'); only the percentage reductions of about 6% and 10% are given
